prompt: Why does the lesson install Newman into the project instead of running it with npx as lesson 5 did?
hint: Where was the version written in lesson 5?

choices.text: npx cannot run Newman more than once
choices.why: npx ran it many times in lesson 5, from its cache.

choices.text: So the version is written in a file every checkout reads
choices.why: Right. package.json and the lock make every machine run the same Newman.

choices.text: A local Newman runs the collection faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; the same program runs either way.

choices.text: boxoffice needs Newman as one of its own dependencies
choices.why: boxoffice still depends on nothing; Newman is a dev dependency.

prompt: What does --save-exact change in package.json?
hint: Compare 6.2.3 with ^6.2.3.

choices.text: It stops npm from writing a package-lock.json
choices.why: The lock was written anyway, as the ls of the project would show.

choices.text: It installs Newman without its dependencies
choices.why: 148 packages were added; dependencies always come along.

choices.text: It writes 6.2.3 rather than a range
choices.why: Right. ^6.2.3 would let a later install take any 6.x.

choices.text: It saves Newman as a dependency instead of a dev dependency
choices.why: --save-dev decides that; --save-exact decides the version string.

prompt: npm reports 19 vulnerabilities and suggests npm audit fix --force. Why does the lesson not run it?
hint: Read what it would install.

choices.text: The vulnerabilities are in boxoffice, which the course keeps unfixed on purpose
choices.why: They are in Newman's dependencies; boxoffice has none.

choices.text: It would install the older Newman 4.6.1
choices.why: Right, for a tool that only runs on your own machines. The finding is recorded and the pinned version kept.

choices.text: --force deletes package.json
choices.why: It rewrites versions; it does not delete the file.

choices.text: Audit reports are always false alarms
choices.why: They are real findings; the question is where the code runs.

prompt: Which of these belong in the git repository?
hint: What does npm ci need, and what does it rebuild?

choices.text: package.json
choices.why: Right: it names the tools.

choices.text: package-lock.json
choices.why: Right: npm ci installs from it.

choices.text: node_modules/
choices.why: npm ci rebuilds it exactly from the lock.

choices.text: results/newman.xml
choices.why: A run leaves it behind; each run writes a new one.

choices.text: .env
choices.why: It holds a secret; lesson 3 put it in .gitignore.

prompt: HEAD one show answered 405. Why is the failed cell of the requests row still 0?
hint: What does that row count as a failure?

choices.text: Newman does not count HEAD requests
choices.why: It counted ten requests, HEAD included.

choices.text: 405 is a success code in Newman's table
choices.why: 405 is a client error; the assertion row failed because of it.

choices.text: A 405 is an answer, not a failed send
choices.why: Right. That cell counts requests that could not be sent. The disagreement shows in the assertions row.

choices.text: The pre-request script retried it until it worked
choices.why: Nothing retries it; it answered 405 once.

prompt: How many requests did the whole run send, counting the one from pm.sendRequest?
hint: The requests row.

prompt: The table shows 11 prerequest-scripts for 9 requests in the file. Where do the extra two come from?
hint: Which requests have a pre-request script of their own?

choices.text: From the two folders without authorization
choices.why: noauth sets no script; the folders have none.

choices.text: From Newman's own setup, which counts as two scripts
choices.why: Newman counts only scripts in the collection.

choices.text: From the token request sent by pm.sendRequest
choices.why: That counts as a request, not as a script.

choices.text: From Create order and Order seats, which make a key
choices.why: Right. The collection's runs before all 9, and those two add their own.

prompt: What exit code did npm run test:api give for the whole collection?
hint: The exit transcript.

choices.text: 0, because 17 of 18 assertions passed
choices.why: One failure is enough for 1.
Right. HEAD one show fails, so the run fails.

choices.text: 405, the status that failed
choices.why: An exit code is not an HTTP status.

choices.text: 18, one per assertion
choices.why: The exit code says whether, not how many.

prompt: A collection with no test scripts runs in a pipeline, and every request answers 500. What does the job show?
hint: What can fail when nothing asserts?

choices.text: Red, because Newman treats any 5xx as a failure
choices.why: Newman judges only through assertions; a 500 is an answer.

choices.text: Green: exit code 0, since nothing asserted anything
choices.why: Right. A green pipeline says only that the tests that exist passed.

choices.text: Neither: Newman refuses to run a collection without tests
choices.why: It runs it, as it ran lesson 4's in this lesson's own words.

choices.text: Red, because the requests row counts the 500s as failed
choices.why: That row counts requests that could not be sent.

prompt: Why does the lesson leave --bail out of the pipeline?
hint: What happens to the failures after the first?

choices.text: --bail makes the exit code 0
choices.why: The bail run exited 1.

choices.text: --bail does not work with the JUnit reporter
choices.why: The bail run wrote a JSON report; reporters work with it.

choices.text: It hides every failure after the first
choices.why: Right. The run stopped at HEAD one show and never reached the orders.

choices.text: GitHub Actions rejects any command with --bail
choices.why: GitHub runs whatever command you write.

prompt: The run with --bail sent requests under how many different request names before it stopped?
hint: jq listed them; one name appears twice.

prompt: Match each reporter to who reads what it writes.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: a CI system showing tests by name

prompt: In the JUnit file, what is one <testcase>?
hint: grep counted 18 of them.

choices.text: One request
choices.why: Requests with tests are testsuites; there were nine.

choices.text: One assertion, one pm.test
choices.why: Right. Eighteen, the same count as the table.

choices.text: One folder of the collection
choices.why: There are five folders, and eighteen test cases.

choices.text: One whole run
choices.why: One run produced the whole file.

prompt: Why should a third-party reporter such as htmlextra get a look before it is installed?
hint: What does a reporter see?

choices.text: It replaces the cli reporter, which cannot be used again
choices.why: --reporters takes a list; cli stays available.

choices.text: It changes the exit code of every run
choices.why: The exit code comes from Newman's results, not from a reporter's page.

choices.text: It sees every request and token
choices.why: Right. It reads every request and response of the run. It is a dependency with access to credentials.

choices.text: It only works inside the Postman app
choices.why: It is a Newman reporter, run from the command line.

prompt: Put the workflow's steps in the order they run.
hint: A fresh machine has nothing yet.

prompt: Why is each action written as actions/checkout@3d3c42e... rather than actions/checkout@v7?
hint: Who can move a tag?

choices.text: GitHub refuses tags in workflow files
choices.why: Most examples use tags, and GitHub runs them.

choices.text: Only a tag moves
choices.why: Right. A tag is a pointer its owner moves at will; a commit hash is fixed. The comment beside it says which release it was.

choices.text: A hash makes the action download faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; what runs is.

choices.text: v7 does not exist yet
choices.why: The comment names v7.0.1, which is a v7.

prompt: Why does the workflow use npm ci instead of npm install?
hint: Which one may change the lock?

choices.text: npm install does not work on Ubuntu runners
choices.why: It works anywhere npm does.

choices.text: npm ci skips Newman's dependencies to save time
choices.why: It installed all 148 packages.

choices.text: npm ci also starts boxoffice
choices.why: Starting boxoffice is its own step.

choices.text: It installs exactly what the lock says
choices.why: Right, and it fails if package.json disagrees. npm install may update the lock instead.

prompt: Why does the report step carry if always()?
hint: When is the report most wanted?

choices.text: So it runs after the collection step failed
choices.why: Right. A failed run is when the report is wanted.

choices.text: So it runs before every other step
choices.why: Steps keep their order; always() is about failure.

choices.text: So the job turns green whatever the tests said
choices.why: The job's colour still comes from the run's exit code.

choices.text: So the report is uploaded on every push to every branch
choices.why: on: decides which pushes run the workflow at all.

prompt: The pipeline's run step fails with every request [errored] and connect ECONNREFUSED. The wait step was deleted last week. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What did the wait step protect against?

choices.text: boxoffice has a new defect that refuses connections
choices.why: Nothing changed in boxoffice; the order of the steps did.

choices.text: The token expired before the run began
choices.why: An expired token is a 401 answer, not a refused connection.

choices.text: Newman ran before boxoffice was listening
choices.why: Right. Starting a server and using it at once is a race; waiting for /health removed it.

choices.text: npm ci installed a different Newman
choices.why: The lock pins 6.2.3, and a version would not refuse connections.

prompt: A teammate wants the pipeline green this week and proposes deleting the HEAD test. What does the course's reasoning recommend?
hint: What is a test that fails until a defect is fixed?

choices.text: Delete it, because a red pipeline teaches people to ignore red
choices.why: The red here is a real defect; deleting the test hides it.

choices.text: Keep it red until boxoffice answers HEAD, or fix boxoffice
choices.why: Right. The test is the defect report, run on every push.

choices.text: Add --bail so the HEAD test stops counting
choices.why: --bail stops at the first failure and still exits 1.

choices.text: Change it to expect 405, which is what boxoffice answers
choices.why: That would assert the defect as correct behaviour.

prompt: ci-local.sh passes on your laptop, but on GitHub npm ci fails saying package.json and package-lock.json are not in sync. What happened?
hint: What did GitHub check out?

choices.text: GitHub's Ubuntu cannot read a lock written on another machine
choices.why: The lock is plain JSON and the same everywhere.

choices.text: The npm cache from setup-node is out of date
choices.why: A stale cache would be downloaded again; it does not make the files disagree.

choices.text: node_modules was not committed
choices.why: It should not be; npm ci builds it from the lock.

choices.text: The lock was not committed with package.json
choices.why: Right. package.json changed and the updated lock stayed behind. Your laptop has the new lock; the repository has the old one.
